guide.title: Endocrine Emergencies
guide.lead: Check the glucose in every patient with altered mental status. Low sugar is quick to kill and quick to fix. High sugar with ketones (DKA) or severe dehydration (HHS) needs fluids and a hospital. Don't forget the steroid-dependent patient in shock.

sections.title: Hypoglycemia
sections.question: Awake and able to swallow safely?
sections.yes: 15–20 g oral glucose; recheck after 15 minutes; repeat if still low; then food.
sections.no: Glucagon 1 mg IM (0.5 mg if under 25 kg) or nasal glucagon 3 mg; or IV dextrose 10%, 100 mL (ALS). Never oral glucose when unresponsive.

sections.title: Don't leave them at home if

groups.title: Recurrence risk
items: Long-acting insulin or an intentional overdose
No one to watch them; can't eat

sections.title: DKA, HHS and adrenal crisis
items: DKA and HHS: fluids (0.9% saline 1 L over the first hour in adults per protocol), monitor, transport
Never stop insulin on sick days; check ketones
Adrenal crisis (known adrenal insufficiency or steroid dependence, shock, vomiting): hydrocortisone 100 mg IM/IV

quiz.q: Type 1 diabetic, unconscious, warm dry skin, fruity breath, deep breathing at 30/min:
A confused diabetic given oral glucose becomes unconscious. Next?
options: Protect the airway, give glucagon IM (or IV dextrose) and transport

quiz.q: Type 2 diabetic, lethargic and very dehydrated, glucose 940 mg/dL, no Kussmaul breathing or fruity breath:
Oral glucose dose for an awake hypoglycemic adult:
Glucagon dose for an unconscious adult:
quiz.explanation: 0.5 mg if under 25 kg; nasal glucagon 3 mg.

quiz.q: Why transport a patient whose hypoglycemia was caused by gliclazide?
quiz.explanation: Same for long-acting insulin and overdoses.

quiz.q: IV dextrose for an adult hypoglycemic (ALS):
A steroid-dependent patient is vomiting and in shock. Think of:

options: Never stop insulin; check glucose and ketones more often

flashcards.question: DKA vs HHS
flashcards.answer: DKA: hyperglycemia + ketones + acidosis, hours, Kussmaul, fruity breath, type 1. HHS: glucose 600 mg/dL (33.3 mmol/L) or more, no significant ketosis, days, profound dehydration, older type 2.

flashcards.question: Signs of hypoglycemia
flashcards.answer: Fast onset, pale cool sweaty skin, tremor, hunger, tachycardia, confusion or odd behaviour, seizures, focal deficits. Glucose below 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L).

flashcards.question: Treating an awake hypoglycemic
flashcards.answer: 15–20 g oral glucose; recheck after 15 minutes; repeat if still low; then food.

flashcards.question: Glucagon
flashcards.answer: 1 mg IM (0.5 mg if under 25 kg), or nasal glucagon 3 mg, when the patient can't swallow safely.

flashcards.question: Kussmaul breathing
flashcards.answer: Deep, fast breathing that blows off CO₂ to compensate for metabolic acidosis, as in DKA.

flashcards.question: The three Ps of hyperglycemia
flashcards.answer: Polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia: from osmotic diuresis.

flashcards.question: Sick-day rules
flashcards.answer: Never stop insulin; check glucose and ketones more often; drink fluids; seek help early if vomiting or unable to eat.

flashcards.question: First step in an altered diabetic patient
flashcards.answer: Check the glucose straight away and treat a low before looking for the cause.

critical.scenario: A type 1 diabetic became confused, then unresponsive. Shallow breathing, pale and sweaty, HR 112. Glucose 32 mg/dL.
critical.question: Management?

options.t: Airway, recovery position, glucagon 1 mg IM (or IV dextrose 10% by ALS), recheck and transport
Oral glucose gel between the cheek and gum
Wait for her to wake up

critical.explanation: Once awake and able to swallow, give oral carbohydrate: glucagon's effect is short.

critical.scenario: A 20-year-old with type 1 diabetes ran out of insulin 3 days ago. Vomiting, abdominal pain, drowsy, warm dry skin, RR 32 and deep, fruity breath. Glucose 480 mg/dL, SpO₂ 97%.
critical.question: Condition and management?

options.t: DKA: airway, IV fluids per protocol, monitor, rapid transport for insulin and electrolytes
Give his own insulin dose and leave
Slow his breathing with a bag

critical.explanation: 0.9% saline 1 L over the first hour in adults per protocol; watch for low potassium arrhythmias.

critical.scenario: A 55-year-old with type 2 diabetes on metformin and glyburide (a sulfonylurea) has eaten little for a week with a UTI. Glucose 65 mg/dL, cool and clammy, confused but swallowing safely.
critical.question: Best treatment?

options.t: 15–20 g oral glucose, recheck after 15 minutes, then transport: the sulfonylurea can cause recurrent lows

options.f: Lows can recur for many hours.

critical.explanation: The infection is a second reason to transport.
